lessons.title: 1.1 · The role and your personal AI roadmap
lessons.summary: Who the AI Value Architect is, why the role exists, and how to build your own AI fluency.

blocks.text:
SAFe describes AI Value Architects as dedicated roles on the Agile Release Train that help it adopt AI. The description draws three boundaries. The role is business-literate without being the business owner, AI-fluent without being the AI developer, and facilitative without being only a facilitator. The course sums up the stance as facilitate, don't fix: a connector and translator.

The public summary gives five areas of focus: coach teams on responsible AI use; find better ways to use existing AI tools; connect business goals with technical execution; facilitate connection across roles and manage risks; and use data to measure success. The size of the solution does not change these responsibilities. Good candidates are people who already connect work and people: Scrum Masters or Team Coaches, Product Managers and Architects.
blocks.title: The role

blocks.text:
The framework cites industry research that puts AI project failure rates above 80 percent, and says failures concentrate in the proof of concept graveyard: promising demos that never reach scaled use. It lists five causes: data not ready, operations not planned, risk not bounded, adoption not engineered, and value not measured.

Notice that none of the five is 'the model was not good enough'. The role exists to bring a systems view that links strategy with technical execution.

The course's Value Maximizer Playbook starts closer to home. Its steps are Audit, Activate, Optimize and Centralize, and its stated aim is to unlock the large share of latent value in AI tools the organisation already owns.
blocks.title: Why the role exists

blocks.text: A personal AI roadmap is the change agent's own learning plan: which AI skills to build, in what order, and through which practice. It starts with an honest check of current skills against what the role needs, then keeps a short learning backlog of skills and experiments, reviewed every few months as tools and the teams' needs change. A useful profile is T-shaped: broad AI literacy, enough to talk with any team about models, retrieval, agents, evaluation, cost and responsible use, plus depth in one area that serves the role.
blocks.title: Your personal AI roadmap

blocks.text: A change agent writes "get better at AI" as a goal and nothing changes. The rewrite is actionable: "use AI to draft the weekly flow report in half the time, and log what works". Each week they try one new capability on a real task, note the result and share useful patterns with the teams. After a month they can explain, with their own examples, where the assistant is reliable and where it misses risks in long documents.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: AI fluency means discussing technical trade-offs in business terms; it does not mean training models or writing production code. The answer that has the change agent building, fixing or deciding for the teams is the wrong one. Learning by reading alone, or by twelve skills at once, is the weak option.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A director asks whether to fine-tune a model or use retrieval for a policy assistant. What should the Value Architect ask first? How often the knowledge changes and whether answers must show their sources; frequent change and citations point to retrieval.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A team asks a question about agents that the Value Architect cannot answer. Instead of guessing, they say so, build a small agent on a safe internal task, learn how it plans and fails, and come back with what they found. The honesty, and the first-hand example, earn more trust than a confident guess would have.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Write three items for your own learning backlog, each with a real task, the AI technique you will try and how you will judge the result.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: (1) summarise my meeting notes with AI and check every claim, judged by minutes saved; (2) compare two prompting approaches on ten real tickets, judged by reviewer edits; (3) build a retrieval assistant over one policy folder, judged by citation accuracy on twenty questions.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: The role sits on the ART: business-literate without being the Business Owner, AI-fluent without being the AI developer, facilitative without being only a facilitator. Candidates: Scrum Masters or Team Coaches, Product Managers, Architects. Personal roadmap: skills check, learning backlog, practice on real tasks, regular review, responsible-use skills alongside technical ones, and sharing what works.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Organizational influence and leadership
lessons.summary: Influence without authority: credibility, champions, sceptics, safety and 'facilitate, don't fix'.

blocks.text:
AI fluency, in the course's words, is the ability to discuss technical trade-offs in business language; its example is the economics of retrieval versus fine-tuning. A director choosing between them needs to hear about cost and freshness, not about embeddings.

A change agent's credibility comes from visible, current practice, which is why the first topic is a personal AI roadmap: regular, deliberate use on real work, with reflection. Influence without authority rests on evidence that matters to the other person. A small result on a team's own problem persuades more than a mandate or an industry statistic.

When adoption stalls, diagnose before prescribing. The gap may be skill, tooling, the process around the tool, or incentives, and each needs a different remedy. When groups talk past each other, the contribution is translation and a shared definition of success.
blocks.title: Building your own capability and influence

blocks.text: The Value Architect rarely has line authority over the teams, so change happens through influence. The most durable source of influence is credibility from helping teams solve problems they care about. It grows through visible wins, honest communication, a network of champions in each team, and alliances in both business and technology. Leadership here is servant leadership: the role succeeds when other people's capability grows, which is the meaning of the course phrase "facilitate, don't fix".
blocks.title: Understand

blocks.text: A senior manager publicly doubts an AI initiative. Rather than asking the sponsor to overrule them, the Value Architect meets the manager, hears that the concern is data quality in their department, and invites them to define what evidence would convince them. The pilot is adjusted to test that. The sceptic becomes one of its most credible supporters.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Escalation, mandates and usage targets look like strong leadership in the options but produce compliance, not commitment. The usual right answer listens first, builds evidence with willing teams and spreads practice through peers.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A sponsor wants one AI tool mandated for all teams next week. What is the best response? Propose a short pilot with willing volunteers and clear criteria, which moves fast and builds evidence.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

Statistics alone, or stories without numbers
Leaders use AI openly, limits included

blocks.title: Tools of influence

blocks.text: Teams start to feel judged for not using AI after a hard push. The Value Architect stops reporting usage by team, shares their own failed experiments, and spends each team's limited time on the blocker that team chooses. Requests for help start to arrive before problems escalate, which shows influence growing.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the better choice: (a) a ranking of teams by AI adoption, or a monthly show-and-tell of AI wins; (b) escalating resistance, or exploring why a team rejects a practice; (c) fixing a team's failing prompt before a demo, or working through it with them.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Show-and-tell. (b) Exploring why, then adapting the practice. (c) Working through it with them, so they can solve the next one.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Influence changes minds; authority compels action. Credibility from real help lasts longest. Engage informal leaders and respected sceptics early. Servant leadership. Facilitate, don't fix. Safety to fail. Allies in business and technology. Avoid becoming a bottleneck.

lessons.title: 1.3 · Diagnosing gaps and enabling collaboration
lessons.summary: Why pilots stall, the five causes, the Value Maximizer Playbook, and connecting roles.

blocks.text: SAFe's public description of the role explains why so many AI pilots end in the proof of concept graveyard: promising demos never reach scale because of gaps in data, operations, risk, adoption or value. The change agent's job is to diagnose which gap is holding a team back before prescribing anything, and to connect the people who can close it. More training is the default prescription, and often the wrong one, because the cause may be process, policy, incentives, trust or data rather than skills.
blocks.title: Understand

rows: People try the tool once and stop
blocks.title: Reading the symptoms

blocks.text: Usage of a coding assistant at Saxby Energy is high, yet delivery is no faster. The Value Architect sits with two teams and finds that the security review rejects most assisted code, which is then rewritten by hand. The gap is the process around the tool. She brings security and the teams together, they agree a short checklist and an automated scan that assisted code must pass, and rework falls. She did not write a line of code or issue a rule.
blocks.title: Worked example · Saxby Energy

blocks.text: Licence counts and usage are not value, and "train everyone again" is rarely the first step. The playbook starts with an audit of what the organisation already owns, not with buying new tools.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Teams have the tools and the skills, but approvals take three weeks. Where is the gap? In the process around the tools.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The course names these steps; the public pages do not describe them. Check this reading against your workbook.

Switch unused capability on and help people start using it
Improve how active AI is used so it delivers more

lessons.title: 2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management
lessons.summary: Mapping stakeholders, interests behind positions, conflict styles, decision rights and alignment artefacts.

blocks.text:
This is the largest domain. Alignment starts with a map of who is affected, what each wants and how much influence each has. A vague mandate such as 'use AI in customer service' has to become a specific outcome with a measure and an owner before anyone can align on it, and success criteria have to be agreed before a pilot starts.

Conflict is information. Legal wanting every output reviewed and product wanting full automation are positions; the interests behind them, safety and speed, can often both be met, for example by reviewing according to risk. Surface objections early. A concern that is not heard in design returns as a veto at release.
blocks.title: Alignment and conflict

rows: Keep satisfied with brief, relevant updates
blocks.title: Power-interest grid

rows: Important issues where both sides' concerns can be fully met
Moderate issues where a quick, fair split is acceptable
Urgent safety or compliance issues needing a firm decision
When the issue matters more to the other side
Trivial issues, or briefly while facts are gathered
blocks.title: Conflict-handling styles

blocks.text: Jesmond Bank wants an assistant that drafts replies to customers. Legal wants every reply reviewed; product wants none reviewed. The Value Architect maps the replies by consequence. Replies about balances and fees can cause financial harm, so a person approves each. Replies that suggest help articles are low risk, so they go out automatically with weekly sampling. Both interests are met. The investment case includes the reviewers' time and the cost per reply at full volume, and funding is released for one product line first.
blocks.title: Worked example · Jesmond Bank

blocks.text: Escalating to the most senior person, or splitting the difference, are the tempting wrong answers. The better answer explores the interests behind each position and designs for both, as with risk-based review.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What separates a position from an interest? A position is what someone demands; an interest is why they demand it.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: One accountable owner, shown in a RACI chart, keeps decisions moving; shared accountability blurs who answers. A decision log records what was decided, why and by whom, with a rule for when a decision may be reopened. "Disagree and commit" lets a group move without unanimity. A small group with clear decision rights, consulting others, decides faster than a twelve-person steering group. Realistic expectations protect alignment from hype.
blocks.title: Decisions that stick

blocks.text: A Business Owner wants an AI feature in three months; the team estimates six. Write the best aligning move.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Agree what smaller outcome can be delivered in three months, fixing the date and shaping scope around the most valuable part. Splitting the difference gives a date nobody believes.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Stakeholder map and power-interest grid. Positions and interests. Five conflict styles. RACI: one Accountable. Decision log. Disagree and commit. Surface conflict early in a shared forum. Link the initiative to a strategic theme.

lessons.title: 2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management
lessons.summary: Rolling-wave plans, decision points, the four risk responses, oversight by harm, drift and Feasibility Filters.

blocks.text:
AI capability and prices change within months, and feasibility is uncertain. So plan in short cycles, each ending in a decision to continue, change or stop, and fund in increments as evidence arrives. A threshold that is missed should trigger that decision. It should not be moved.

The course's Feasibility Filters exist to de-risk an initiative before code is written. The details are not public, but the timing is the point: test for the blocking problem while a change of direction is cheap.

Bound each risk by asking what the worst outcome of a wrong answer is and who catches it. Match oversight to consequence: human approval where an error causes real harm, monitoring and sampling where it is harmless and reversible. Typical AI risks are plausible but wrong output, data sent where it should not go, retrieval that ignores document permissions, and agents that can be manipulated into actions. Least privilege and approval for irreversible actions limit the last.
blocks.title: Adaptive planning and risk

rows: Not using AI for medical diagnoses at all
Human review of replies that could cause financial harm
Insurance or contract terms for a vendor outage
Living with rare harmless tagging errors
blocks.title: Four responses to a risk

blocks.text: An initiative is unsure whether its data can support the use case. The first increment tests the data as cheaply as possible, with kill criteria agreed in advance. The data holds up, so the next increment builds a thin end-to-end version for twenty users, and the plan is revised at the decision point that follows.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: A twelve-month plan that fixes scope, model and vendor up front is the wrong answer in a field this uncertain. So is oversight set by cost or seniority instead of by the harm a wrong output could cause.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is model drift, and how is it caught? Performance falling as real-world data changes; caught by monitoring quality against a baseline over time, for example with a fixed evaluation set.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Feasibility Filters de-risk an initiative before code is written, for example by asking whether the data is available, good enough and allowed to be used. Evaluation sets of real cases with expected results are run before each change and regularly in use. Pin model versions where possible and re-run evaluations before upgrading. Keep a feature toggle to switch a misbehaving feature off, and a fallback way of working for outages. Revisit the risk register every PI, because risks change as the solution, data and usage change.
blocks.title: Controls that keep AI safe in use

blocks.text: During a pilot, users start pasting confidential data into prompts. The first response is to reduce the risk with clear guidance and data controls, not to accept it or cancel without discussion. The register gains an adoption risk, the guidance is published, and the next review checks whether the behaviour stopped.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the response: (a) buying insurance against vendor outages; (b) deciding not to automate hiring decisions; (c) adding a person to review high-value refunds.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Transfer. (b) Avoid. (c) Reduce.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Rolling-wave planning; short cycles ending in decisions; kill criteria; pre-mortems. Avoid, reduce, transfer, accept. Oversight proportional to harm; start high-risk uses with a person in the loop. Drift, evaluation sets, version pinning, toggles, fallbacks. Translate risk into business terms for leaders.

lessons.title: 2.3 · The investment case and governance
lessons.summary: Total cost of ownership, incremental funding, governance that keeps flow, NIST, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act.

blocks.text:
A sound case states a baseline, the expected change and how it will be measured. It counts the costs that continue after launch: evaluation, monitoring, maintenance and human review. It examines how usage-based cost grows with volume, because a pilot that is cheap for fifty users may not be at fifty thousand. 'Hours saved' is a benefit only when it turns into an outcome.

The retrieval versus fine-tuning trade-off is the course's own example of AI fluency. Retrieval keeps answers current and can cite sources, so it suits knowledge that changes. Fine-tuning has an up-front cost that pays back for a stable, specialised behaviour at high volume.
blocks.title: The investment case

rows: The measured state before the change
The outcome expected and how it will be measured
Build, run, monitor, evaluate and support costs, including human review
Named, so the riskiest can be tested first
Small increments released as evidence grows
blocks.title: A sound AI investment case

blocks.text:
Good governance sets guardrails once and lets teams decide inside them: published criteria for data, security and permitted use, so a team gets a fast and consistent answer. A committee that approves every use case creates a queue and invites workarounds. Accountability stays with the person who makes a decision; AI output is an input.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary guidance organised around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. It is not a law, and following it does not by itself establish compliance with the AI Act.
blocks.title: Governance that keeps flow

blocks.text: From the European Commission's AI Act page, read on 14 November 2026.
rows: CV-sorting software for recruitment; credit scoring
Allowed with duties: risk management, data quality, logging, documentation, human oversight, robustness
People must be told; AI-generated content must be identifiable
Spam filters; AI in video games

blocks.text: Emotion recognition in workplaces and schools is among the prohibited practices. Whether and how deeply the course covers the Act is not public.

blocks.text: NIST's framework is voluntary guidance; the AI Act is law. "Hours saved" is a benefit only if the time is used for something valuable. A single central board approving every use case is the slow answer; risk tiers with published criteria are the scalable one.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A company uses an AI tool built by another firm in its own HR process. What is its role under the AI Act? Deployer; the firm that built it is the provider.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: An AI inventory records which systems exist, what they do, their risk tier and their owner. Model cards record intended use, limits and test results. ISO/IEC 42001 specifies an AI management system, alongside ISO/IEC 27001 for information security. Governance covers the prompts and data sent to external services as well as outputs, requires evaluations to be re-run before a model is switched, and asks for a data protection check before AI is connected to personal data.
blocks.title: Governance artefacts

blocks.text: A governance board meets quarterly and teams wait months for approvals. It publishes risk tiers and simple criteria, delegates low-risk decisions to teams, and keeps high-risk cases for itself, with a named owner and risk and legal involved by policy. Approvals for most uses now take days.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: An investment case shows high value but leaves out the reviewers who check outputs. What is wrong, and what else should it compare against?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Running costs are understated, flattering the return. It should also compare a simpler non-AI improvement to the same process, as well as doing nothing.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: TCO over the solution's life; usage-based costs grow with volume. Fund in small steps. Guardrails with decentralised decisions. Risk tiers. AI inventory, model cards, ISO/IEC 42001. NIST: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage, voluntary. AI Act: risk-based, provider and deployer duties, dates.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text:
Generic answer: escalate the conflict to the senior leader. Better answer: explore interests and design for both.

A manager deciding: a committee approving each use case. The guardrail approach lets teams decide within limits.

Wrong control: a disclaimer where a human check is needed, or double approval where monitoring is enough.

Wrong law: NIST is voluntary; the AI Act is law. Recruitment screening is high risk, not prohibited. Workplace emotion recognition is prohibited, not high risk.

Wrong dates: December 2027 is for stand-alone high-risk uses; August 2028 is for AI embedded in regulated products.

lessons.title: Lab · AI Act risk levels and oversight
lessons.summary: Classify use cases by AI Act risk level and choose the level of human oversight.

blocks.text: For each case, decide the AI Act risk level and the oversight you would design, then read the answer. Exam questions in this domain often hinge on one distinction: prohibited versus high risk, or transparency duties versus high-risk duties.
blocks.title: How to use this lab

blocks.text: Answer: high risk, because employment uses are listed as high risk. Oversight: a person reviews the shortlist; the provider's documentation and logging duties apply, and the deployer must use it as instructed with human oversight.
blocks.title: Case 1: an AI that sorts job applications

blocks.text: Answer: transparency risk. Users must be told they are dealing with AI. Oversight: sampling of conversations and a route to a person.
blocks.title: Case 2: a customer chatbot on a retail website

blocks.text: Answer: prohibited, since emotion recognition in the workplace is banned except for medical or safety reasons. It is not merely high risk.
blocks.title: Case 3: an AI that infers employees' emotions in meetings

blocks.text: Answer: minimal risk. Oversight: automatic use with monitoring and periodic sampling.
blocks.title: Case 4: an AI that suggests tags for internal help articles

lessons.title: 3.1 · The solution lifecycle, iterative delivery and quick wins
lessons.summary: Sense, Discover, Design, Deliver; small end-to-end increments; choosing and measuring quick wins.

blocks.text:
The course names four phases of the AI-Native solution lifecycle: Sense, Discover, Design and Deliver. Its public description says they turn a vague mandate into a finalized, cross-functional AI-Native Value Blueprint, and that planning the whole lifecycle, from demo to production, is the way out of the proof of concept graveyard.

Cross-functional matters because the five causes of stalled pilots, data, operations, risk, adoption and value, sit in different functions. A design agreed by technology alone leaves the others to object later.
blocks.title: The lifecycle and the blueprint

blocks.text:
Deliver in small increments that work end to end for a narrow scope: one policy area, one step of a process, a small group of users. Start by assisting people and extend toward automation as evidence allows.

A good quick win is a frequent, low-risk task with a visible, measurable result. Its value is partly the benefit and partly the evidence and momentum it creates. It does not prove that the hardest use case will work, and governance still applies.
blocks.title: Iterative delivery and quick wins

blocks.text: An invoice solution grows in steps: first AI suggests fields for a clerk to confirm, then it fills low-risk fields automatically, then it routes exceptions to the right team, and only then does it process routine invoices end to end. Each step adds responsibility only after the previous one has proved reliable.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Automating the whole process in the first release, or rolling out to every region at once, is the tempting wrong answer. So is a high-profile, high-risk first use case. Choose small, low-risk, visible work tied to a real need.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which first increment fits a policy assistant? Answers for one topic area, with sources, for a small group of users.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A walking skeleton connects data, model, workflow and interface in the thinnest working form, so integration problems appear early. A minimum viable product tests whether the core idea works and is wanted, at low cost. Feature toggles release to some users and switch off fast if needed. Measured quick wins, with a baseline, become evidence that builds trust and funding for harder use cases.
blocks.title: Tools for small, safe steps

blocks.text: An insurance company new to AI picks summarising long claim files for adjusters to review as its first win, not automatic approvals. It measures handling time before and after, shares the result, and uses the trust it earns to fund a second use case.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: A first increment gets mixed feedback. What should the team do?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Find what drove the feedback, by user group, and adjust the next increment. Stopping or ignoring the feedback wastes the reason for releasing early.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Lifecycle phases: Sense, Discover, Design, Deliver, producing the AI-Native Value Blueprint. Small end-to-end increments. Quick wins: small, low-risk, visible, real need, measured. Walking skeleton, MVP, feature toggles. Expand region by region.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Readiness and momentum
lessons.summary: Data, operations, risk and adoption readiness before go-live, and how to keep momentum until habits form.

blocks.text:
Before delivery, check readiness against the same five causes. Is the data complete, accessible and permitted for this use? Has someone been named to monitor quality after launch and respond when it degrades? Is the risk bounded? Have the people whose work will change been involved? Is there a baseline and a measure?

Readiness is rarely complete. The usual decision is to limit scope and close the gap, not to ignore it or stop. Momentum is sustained by a regular cadence of visible results and shared learning.
blocks.title: Readiness and momentum

rows: Is the data current, complete and allowed for this use?
Who owns monitoring, incidents and updates after launch?
Are controls, oversight and an incident owner in place?
Did users help shape it, and do they know how it fits their work?
blocks.title: Go-live readiness

blocks.text: Upwell Health wants an assistant that answers staff questions on clinical policy. The readiness check finds the policies are current for two departments only, and nobody owns monitoring. The first increment covers those two departments, answers with sources, and goes to twenty staff. A named owner reviews flagged answers weekly. In the design workshop, clinicians ask for a visible 'not sure' response, which becomes part of the blueprint. After four weeks of results, two more departments are added.
blocks.title: Worked example · Upwell Health

blocks.text: "The technology works, so launch to everyone" ignores the people and operations sides. Hiding a failed readiness check, or launching on bad data and fixing it later, is never the answer; reduce scope to what is ready.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Data is ready and the model works, but support has not been trained. What should happen? Train support first, or launch small enough for them to handle.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Momentum fades after a good start unless people keep seeing progress. Regular demos to users, visible results with credit to those who achieved them, and involving frontline users before go-live keep people engaged until the new way of working becomes a habit. Readiness is not a one-off: regular reviews of data, quality and user feedback keep the solution fit as things change.
blocks.title: Keeping momentum

blocks.text: A go-live date is fixed, but data readiness has failed. What is the best option?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Launch a reduced scope that the ready data supports, and tell the steering group what was cut and why.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Four readiness checks: data, operations, risk, adoption, plus value. A named operations owner. Readiness checklist of agreed criteria. Reduce scope rather than launch unready. Momentum from regular visible results. Involve users before go-live.

lessons.title: 3.3 · Facilitating the Design phase
lessons.summary: Who is in the room, how to reach decisions, what the design must cover, and the facilitator's stance.

blocks.text:
The exam lists facilitating the Design phase as a topic. A design session needs business, technology, data, risk and the people who will use the solution in the room together. It needs room to generate options and then a way to converge: criteria agreed in advance and a decision step in the agenda.

The facilitator frames options and trade-offs so the group that owns the decision can make it. The design itself covers more than a model and a prompt: the changed workflow, where people check the output, and how success is measured.
blocks.title: Facilitating the design phase

blocks.text: In a design workshop, a senior architect asks the Value Architect to pick the model. The Value Architect instead frames the options and their trade-offs and asks the owners to decide against criteria agreed at the start. When data science and operations disagree about retraining frequency, the trade-off is made explicit and the group agrees who decides and on what evidence.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: The facilitator who decides for the group, or who just takes notes after the experts decide, has the role wrong. A design that covers only the model and the prompt leaves out where the value comes from: the changed workflow.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A session produces a long list of ideas and nothing chosen. What was missing? Agreed criteria and a decision step, such as dot voting against those criteria.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

rows: Value comes from new ways of working, not the model alone
Where people review, approve or take over
What the solution may read and act on
How we will know it helped
blocks.title: What the design must cover

blocks.text: A workshop with twenty attendees stalls. The facilitator splits them into small breakout groups, each prototypes the changed workflow as a rough mock-up, and the groups bring proposals back for a decision against the agreed criteria.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Who needs to be in a design workshop for an AI claims assistant?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Business owners, technology, data, risk or compliance, and the people who will use it, here the claims handlers.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Discover comes before Design. Cross-functional room. Agreed criteria, then a decision. Frame options; owners decide. Design the workflow, checkpoints, data, controls and measures. Rough prototypes tested with users. Breakouts for large groups.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Storytelling for impact
lessons.summary: Story structure, protagonists, before-and-after evidence and tailoring for audiences.

blocks.text:
The course's AI-Powered Story Amplifier turns technical success metrics into a narrative for senior leaders, in order to secure funding and adoption. The underlying skill is translation. 'F1 of 0.91' means nothing to a finance director. 'Nine in ten claims are now routed without manual triage' does.

A structure that works: the problem the audience recognises, what was done, the measured result, and the decision you need from them. A concrete example of one person or team makes the numbers credible. Adapt emphasis and language to the audience, and keep the facts the same for everyone.
blocks.title: Storytelling for impact

rows: Claims took nine days, and customers complained
Adjusters got AI summaries of long files to review
Claims now close in four days, with no rise in reopened cases
One adjuster's team and a customer whose claim was paid sooner
This budget gets us five more sites by June
blocks.title: A story for impact

blocks.text: A team tells executives its model "reached 0.91 F1". The rewrite opens with the outcome the sponsor cares about, claims closing in four days instead of nine, shows one simple before-and-after chart, names the team whose work changed, admits what did not work, and ends with a specific ask.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Model accuracy is not the story; what changed for customers or costs is. Twenty metrics bury the result; lead with the two or three that matter to this audience. Tailoring changes emphasis and language, never the facts.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What should the storyteller be ready to show behind "saved 5,000 hours"? How it was measured and what the time went to.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The same pilot is presented to engineers and to the finance director. For engineers, the emphasis is the changed workflow and the remaining errors; for finance, cost per claim net of running costs. The facts are identical in both.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Write an opening line for a story to frontline staff about an AI tool.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: "From Monday, the first draft of each reply is ready when you open the case, so you can spend your time on the tricky ones." It says what changes in their day and how it helps.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: The AI-Powered Story Amplifier turns technical metrics into a story that secures funding and adoption. Structure: situation, change, result, protagonist, ask. Lead with the audience's goal. Before and after. Admit limits. Exaggeration destroys credibility.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Measuring value
lessons.summary: Baselines, leading and lagging indicators, balanced measures, counterfactuals and value across the stream.

blocks.text:
Using data to measure success is one of the five areas of the role, and value not measured is one of the five causes of stalled pilots.

Start with a baseline, the measured state before the change. Pair a leading indicator, an early signal such as weekly use, with a lagging outcome, such as resolution time or satisfaction. Keep inputs and activity apart from results: licences bought and prompts sent are not value. Adoption is not value either; high usage with no change in the outcome means the tool is used for the wrong things or its output is discarded downstream. Report quality next to speed, so that a gain in output is not hiding a rise in defects.
blocks.title: Measuring value

rows: Handling time and quality before launch
The starting point for any claim
Share of suggestions accepted each day
Shows speed did not cost quality
blocks.title: Kinds of measure

blocks.text: An assistant for support agents at Bramhall Bank reaches 85 percent weekly use in a month, and the sponsor wants to announce success. The Value Architect compares resolution time with the baseline taken before launch: no change. Sitting with agents, she finds they use the assistant to rephrase replies, not to find answers. The team changes the workflow so the assistant proposes an answer with its source at the start of each case. Six weeks later resolution time is down by a fifth. Her report to the board opens with one customer's case, gives the before and after figures, notes that reopened cases did not rise, and asks for funding to extend to a second team.
blocks.title: Worked example · Bramhall Bank

blocks.text: Usage is adoption, not value. Measures chosen after the pilot tend to be the ones that look good; agree them first. A precise annual return from one month of data is a guess.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A pilot reports faster claims handling, but no measurement was taken before launch. What can it claim? Little, since there is nothing to compare against.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The counterfactual is what would have happened without the solution; comparing similar groups with and without the tool estimates it. Report by group when results differ, for example experienced staff against new starters. Measure value across the value stream: if the benefit lands in another department's budget, it is still value. A value hypothesis states the expected outcome in measurable terms so the initiative can be stopped or scaled on evidence.
blocks.title: Trustworthy evidence

blocks.text: Choose a balanced pair of measures for an AI coding assistant.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Lead time for changes, with defect rates alongside. Lines of code and licence counts are activity.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Baseline first. Leading and lagging indicators. Speed plus quality. Agree measures before the pilot. Counterfactual and comparison groups. Report by group. Value across the stream. Value hypothesis.

lessons.title: 4.3 · Communicating results and making change last
lessons.summary: Balanced updates, channels by audience, cadence, the 'so what', and reinforcing new habits.

blocks.text:
Report on a regular cadence, including when there is little to show. When a pilot misses its target, state the result, what was learned and the recommended decision. An early, cheap 'no' is a return on the experiment. Early figures should be labelled as early, with a date for firmer evidence.

A tool that is deployed and trained on is not yet a change. People return to the old way unless processes, measures and leadership behaviour reinforce the new one. When people fear the change, tell them what will change in their work, what will not, and how they can shape it. The change is embedded when new work is designed with it by default, without a special programme.
blocks.title: Communicating results and making change last

blocks.text: A sponsor asks for "just the good news". The Value Architect explains that hidden bad news surfaces later at a worse moment for the sponsor, and sends a balanced update: what worked, what did not, and what happens next, linked to the outcomes agreed at the start.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Reporting only the successful team, or waiting for good news before reporting, is the wrong answer. A stopped initiative is communicated as an evidence-based decision with lessons, not hidden or spun.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is the 'so what' of a result? What the finding means for the listener's goals, which turns a number into a reason to act.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

rows: Short demo in their team meeting
blocks.title: Channels by audience

blocks.text: Rumours spread that a pilot failed when in fact it met its goals. The Value Architect shares the actual results openly and promptly, through champions in each area, rather than asking managers to stop the discussion.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: A tool helps one team a lot and another not at all. What should the update say?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Both results, with the reasons as far as they are known, and what will be tried next for the second team. An average would hide the difference.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Balanced updates on a regular cadence. Link results to agreed outcomes. Say the next decision. Tailor channel and emphasis, not facts. Results dashboards for visibility. Reinforce change with updated processes, measures and recognition; new work designed with AI by default shows it has lasted.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text:
Generic answer: report the model's accuracy. This course's answer: say what changed for customers or costs.

Wrong measure: usage as the goal. Usage is a leading indicator; the outcome is the value.

Wrong reporting: showing whichever metric improved, or waiting for good news.

Wrong idea of change: rollout plus training. Without reinforcement, people revert.

Wrong claim: a precise annual return from one month of data.

questions.explanation: The useful answer links the technical choice to cost and freshness, which is what the director is deciding on. questions.prompt: A change agent at Ormsby Rail wants to build her own AI capability over the next quarter. Which plan is the strongest?

Read about each model release and wait for a formal course
Buy several tools and compare their features in a table
Ask the team to report what they learn each month

questions.prompt: Why does a personal AI roadmap matter for someone leading AI adoption?

options.text: Certification bodies require one before each renewal

It replaces the AI strategy of the whole organisation
Credibility with teams comes from visible, current practice

questions.explanation: People follow a change agent who demonstrably uses the tools and keeps learning. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI Value Architect at Pargeter Media has no line authority over the teams she supports. Which approach to influence fits best?

Show a working improvement on a team's own problem and let them judge it
Wait for teams to ask for help
Publish a policy and audit compliance

questions.explanation: Influence without authority rests on evidence, relevance and trust, and a result on the team's own pain is the most persuasive evidence. questions.prompt: Senior engineers at Quillfeather Bank are sceptical that AI helps with their legacy code. How should a change agent respond first?

options.text: Present industry statistics on the productivity gains reported elsewhere
Escalate their resistance to leadership
Ask what would convince them and run a small test on their code
Exclude them from the pilot

questions.prompt: Which stakeholder is most useful to engage early in an AI adoption effort?

options.text: An enthusiast with little standing among the delivery teams
A vendor representative
A manager who is leaving soon
A respected sceptic whose concerns expose real risks

questions.explanation: A respected sceptic brings the objections that would otherwise appear later, and their eventual support carries weight with peers. Enthusiasm without standing does not spread. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Organizational influence and leadership”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Adoption of a coding assistant at Ravenscar Travel is flat. What should the change agent do before proposing a remedy?

Replace the assistant with another vendor's product
Schedule more training sessions for each team
Diagnose the gap: skills, tooling, process or incentives

questions.explanation: Flat adoption has several possible causes, and the remedy for a skills gap differs from the remedy for a blocked workflow or a missing incentive. questions.prompt: Teams at Saxby Energy use the approved assistant, but security reviews reject its output and the work is redone by hand. Where is the gap?

options.text: In the process around the tool, not in individual skill
In the size of the licence pool
In the capability of the model
In the motivation of the developers who are using the assistant

questions.prompt: Data scientists and product managers at Tiverton Health describe the same pilot in incompatible terms and blame each other for delay. What is the Value Architect's most useful contribution?

Move the pilot to a single group

Translate between the groups and agree a shared definition of success

questions.explanation: The role is a connector and translator, so its contribution is a common language and a shared outcome. questions.prompt: Which activity is the clearest example of finding better ways to use existing AI tools?

Building a custom model from scratch

questions.prompt: What does the course's Value Maximizer Playbook aim to unlock?

Unused potential in AI tools the organisation already owns

questions.prompt: In which order does the Value Maximizer Playbook name its four steps?

questions.prompt: An organisation at Underhill Logistics does not know which AI features its existing licences include or who uses them. Which playbook step addresses this?

questions.prompt: A team at Vandermeer Pay has found a way of prompting that halves its review time. Under the playbook's last step, what should happen?

questions.prompt: A team lead at Wetherby Rail asks the Value Architect to fix a failing prompt before a demo. What response develops the team?

questions.prompt: A Value Architect notices that every team brings its AI questions to her and none to each other. What does this indicate?

She is succeeding, since the demand for her help continues to grow
She has become a bottleneck, and peers should share knowledge
The teams need more tools

questions.prompt: Developers at Yarborough Bank paste customer records into a public AI tool to save time. What should the Value Architect do first?

Ban AI tools across the train

questions.prompt: Leaders at Zeller Insurance ask the Value Architect to prove AI adoption by counting licences issued. What is the weakness of that measure?

It counts access, not use or results

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows that a change agent's coaching is working?

options.text: Teams give the sessions high ratings
Teams attend each of the coaching sessions they are offered
Teams request more licences
Teams apply AI to new tasks without asking for help

questions.prompt: A product manager wants an AI feature because a competitor has one. What question should a Value Architect ask first?

questions.prompt: Two teams at Abbotsford Media use different AI tools for the same task and distrust each other's results. What enables collaboration best?

questions.prompt: Which topic does the exam list under Developing the AI-Native Change Agent?

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the systems view this role brings?

questions.prompt: Match each quality in the role description to the boundary it is paired with.

options.text: Only a facilitator

questions.prompt: What is a personal AI roadmap?

questions.prompt: Which item belongs at the start of a Value Architect's personal AI roadmap?

An honest check of current skills against the role's needs

questions.prompt: Why should a change agent learn AI by applying it to real work rather than only taking courses?

questions.prompt: A Value Architect wants to stay current in a field that changes monthly. Which habit helps most?

Reading each vendor's announcements in full as soon as they appear
Waiting for an annual training course to catch up
A short weekly slot to try one new capability on a real task

questions.explanation: Small, regular experiments on real work keep skills current without overwhelming the person. questions.prompt: Which skill does AI fluency mainly add to a Value Architect's role?

Explaining what AI can and cannot do, in plain terms

questions.prompt: A Value Architect is asked whether an AI tool can read scanned contracts reliably. What is the best way to answer?

Quote the vendor's brochure, which claims very high accuracy rates
Test it on a sample of real documents and report results
Say yes, since modern AI can read any document format

questions.prompt: Why should a change agent learn how AI outputs are evaluated?

questions.prompt: Which practice shows a change agent applying AI to their own work responsibly?

Drafting a stakeholder update with AI and checking every claim
Letting AI send stakeholder updates without reading them first
Using AI only for tasks that nobody will ever review

questions.explanation: Responsible personal use means using approved tools, keeping confidential data safe and checking outputs before they reach others. questions.prompt: What does a T-shaped AI skill profile mean for a Value Architect?

questions.prompt: A change agent's roadmap lists twelve skills to master this quarter. What is the main risk?

Too much at once leaves little time to practise each
Skills cannot be learned within a quarter at all
Twelve skills are too few for the role to be credible

questions.prompt: How should a Value Architect decide which AI skill to build next?

By the skill that takes the least time to learn
By the topics that the certification exam lists last
By the gaps that most limit the teams they support

questions.prompt: A Value Architect has found a prompt pattern that cuts drafting time in half. What should they do with it?

Share it with examples, so others can reuse and improve it
Keep it private to stay the team's most valuable expert
Patent it as intellectual property belonging to the Value Architect

questions.explanation: Spreading what works is central to the role: a shared pattern with examples lets other teams gain the same benefit and improve it. questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a learning backlog in a personal AI roadmap?

To list the AI tools the company has rejected

questions.prompt: Which experiment fits a change agent's skill-building best?

Build a full production system alone in a weekend
Ask a vendor to run the experiment and send a report

Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A change agent finds that an AI summary tool misses key risks in long documents. What does this teach about AI fluency?

Knowing where a tool fails matters as much as its strengths

Long documents should be cut to one page before use

questions.explanation: Fluency includes knowing the failure modes of tools, so the change agent can advise teams where human checks are needed. questions.prompt: Which evidence best shows progress on a personal AI roadmap?

options.text: The length of the prompts the person writes
A badge from a short online quiz on common AI terms and jargon
Real tasks done better or faster with AI, with examples
The number of AI webinars attended this year

questions.explanation: Progress is shown by changed work, with concrete examples others can learn from. Attendance and badges show activity, not capability. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · The role and your personal AI roadmap”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does a Value Architect need to understand the cost of running AI solutions?

To audit each team's travel and training budgets

questions.prompt: A Value Architect wants to understand agents better before advising teams on them. What is the most useful step?

Read the marketing material of three different agent vendors

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the role of a personal AI roadmap in leading change?

It sets the AI budget for the train for the year

questions.explanation: Change agents earn credibility by visibly learning and applying AI themselves; a roadmap makes that learning deliberate and shareable. questions.prompt: A Value Architect is unsure whether retrieval or fine-tuning suits a use case. What should they ask first?

questions.prompt: Which mindset best supports skill-building in a fast-moving field like AI?

A competitive mindset that keeps knowledge private

questions.prompt: A team asks the Value Architect a question about AI agents that they cannot answer. What is the best response?

questions.prompt: Why should a personal AI roadmap include responsible-use skills as well as technical ones?

questions.prompt: Which way of tracking a personal AI roadmap is most useful?

A spreadsheet of the AI articles read this year
A short log of experiments, results and next steps
A monthly report of the tools installed on the laptop

questions.explanation: Logging experiments, what happened and what to try next turns practice into learning and gives material to share with teams. Reading lists and installed tools measure inputs. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · The role and your personal AI roadmap”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A Value Architect's roadmap goal is 'get better at AI'. Which rewrite makes it actionable?

Learn about every new AI model that is released
Use AI to draft weekly flow reports in half the time

questions.prompt: Why is it risky for a change agent to rely on a single AI tool for all their learning?

questions.prompt: Which task is the best first practice project for a change agent who is new to AI?

Writing the company's AI policy with AI and no review
Summarising their own meeting notes and checking the result

questions.explanation: A frequent, low-risk task on one's own material gives safe practice and quick feedback. questions.prompt: What does it signal when a change agent can explain an AI limitation with a real example from their own work?

questions.prompt: A Value Architect wants feedback on whether their AI coaching is helping. Whom should they ask?

questions.prompt: Why should a change agent revisit their AI roadmap every few months?

questions.prompt: Which source of influence lasts longest for a change agent without line authority?

questions.prompt: Which action builds a network of AI champions across an ART?

questions.prompt: The same assistant also suggests internal article tags, where mistakes are harmless and easy to correct. Which level of oversight is proportionate?

options.text: No monitoring at all
Review by the legal team
Approval of each tag by two reviewers before it is published
Automatic use with monitoring and periodic sampling

questions.explanation: Oversight should match the consequence of error; low-risk, reversible outputs can flow with monitoring. Double approval for tags spends scarce attention where it prevents nothing. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team at Kirkby Pay plans to send customer transaction data to an external model API. What must be settled first?

Whether the API's response time is fast enough for the feature
Whether the team has enough licences
Whether the prompt is short enough

questions.explanation: Data protection obligations decide whether the design is allowed at all, so they come before performance. A fast answer built on a prohibited data flow has to be thrown away. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A retrieval assistant at Lanchester Health can read any document on the shared drive. Which risk is most direct?

options.text: Users may see content they are not authorised to see
The model may need retraining
The index may grow large
Users may find that their answers arrive a little more slowly

questions.explanation: If retrieval ignores document permissions, the assistant becomes a way around access control. Retrieval should enforce the same permissions as the source system. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An agent at Maddox Logistics can read emails and also issue refunds. Which design principle limits the damage of a manipulated instruction?

options.text: A longer system prompt that tells the agent to behave honestly
A more capable model
A faster rollback of the model version
Least privilege, with approval for irreversible actions

questions.explanation: Limiting what the agent may do and requiring approval before irreversible actions contains the effect of a prompt injection. questions.prompt: Which risk is specific to generative AI and absent from conventional software?

options.text: Downtime of a hosting provider
Plausible output that is factually wrong
Licences that expire
Defects introduced by a change to the code

questions.explanation: Generative models can produce fluent, confident and false statements, so their output needs grounding or verification. The other risks apply to any software system. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which cost is most often missed in the investment case for an AI solution?

options.text: The licence fee for the model during the first month of the pilot
The cost of the demo
The salary of the sponsor
Ongoing evaluation, monitoring and maintenance after launch

questions.explanation: Running an AI solution includes monitoring quality, handling drift, updating prompts and data, and human review, which often exceed the build cost over time. questions.prompt: A pilot at Norham Retail costs little per day with fifty users. What must the investment case examine before scaling to fifty thousand?

options.text: Which colour scheme the interface uses
How usage-based cost grows with volume
Whether the pilot users enjoyed taking part
How many slides the case has

questions.explanation: Model usage is typically priced per unit of text processed, so cost scales with users and requests. A pilot that is cheap at fifty users can be uneconomic at scale. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: From a cost point of view, when is fine-tuning easier to justify than retrieval?

options.text: When answers must cite their sources
When a stable, specialised behaviour is needed at high volume
When the source documents are revised by their owners each week
When the budget for data preparation is zero

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning has an up-front cost that pays back when the behaviour is stable and used heavily. questions.prompt: Which statement belongs in a sound investment case for an AI initiative?

options.text: A list of the features of the chosen model
A baseline, the expected change, and how it will be measured
A promise that the solution pays back within a quarter
A comparison with a competitor's press release

questions.explanation: A case that names the current baseline and the measurable change can be checked later. A promised payback without a baseline cannot be verified. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Oxenhope Energy want to fund ten AI pilots at once. What is the stronger investment approach?

options.text: Fund the cheapest ten ideas
Hold all funding until one vendor is chosen
Fund all ten in full, so that each one of them can keep to its schedule
Fund a few in small increments and release more as evidence arrives

questions.explanation: Incremental funding tied to evidence limits loss on ideas that fail and moves money to those that work. Full funding for ten pilots is how the proof of concept graveyard fills. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An investment case lists 'hours saved' as its single gain. What is the weakness?

options.text: Saved hours are a benefit only if they turn into an outcome
Saved hours should be reported weekly
Saved hours apply to developers alone
Saved hours are too difficult for a finance team to count at all

questions.explanation: Time saved has value when it becomes shorter lead time, more output or lower cost. Otherwise it is a capacity estimate that never reaches the result leaders care about. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which governance arrangement supports both speed and safety for AI use?

options.text: A ban on external models
No rules until a problem occurs
A committee that approves each AI use case before any work starts
Clear guardrails that teams work within without asking each time

questions.explanation: Guardrails set the limits once and let teams decide inside them, which keeps flow and control together. Approval of every case creates a queue and encourages people to work around it. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team asks whether it may use a new AI tool. Which answer reflects good governance?

options.text: Use it quietly until someone elsewhere in the organisation objects to it
Check it against the published criteria for data, security and use
Wait for the annual policy review
Ask the vendor whether it is safe

questions.explanation: Published criteria let teams get a fast, consistent answer. Quiet use without a check is how unapproved tools spread and data leaves the organisation. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who stays accountable for a decision that an AI system recommended?

options.text: The team that wrote the prompt
The person or role that acted on it
The AI system itself
The vendor that supplied the model

questions.explanation: Accountability stays with people; AI output is an input to a human decision. Vendors carry contractual duties, but they do not own the organisation's decisions. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which four functions form the core of the NIST AI RMF?

Audit, Activate, Optimize, Centralize
Plan, Do, Check, Act

questions.explanation: The NIST AI RMF is organised around Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. questions.prompt: What is the status of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?

options.text: It is intended for voluntary use
It applies to government agencies alone
It is a certification scheme
It is a binding federal regulation

questions.explanation: NIST describes the framework as intended for voluntary use to help manage AI risks and build trustworthiness. It is guidance, unlike the EU AI Act, which is law. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Source: NIST · AI Risk Management Framework.

questions.prompt: How does the EU AI Act classify AI systems?

By the country of the provider
By the type of model architecture
By the size of the provider company

questions.explanation: The Act takes a risk-based approach with four levels: unacceptable, high, transparency and minimal risk. questions.prompt: Which four risk levels does the European Commission describe for the AI Act?

Unacceptable, high, transparency, and minimal or no risk
Banned, licensed, registered and exempt

questions.explanation: The Commission describes unacceptable risk, high risk, transparency risk, and minimal or no risk. The other sets resemble common risk scales but are not the Act's categories. questions.prompt: A recruiter at Penhallow Group plans to use AI to sort job applications. Which AI Act risk level does the Commission give as the example for this?

High risk
Minimal risk
Unacceptable risk

questions.prompt: A retailer at Quinton Stores deploys a customer chatbot. What does the AI Act's transparency duty require?

Users are shown the system prompt in each chat

Users are told they are interacting with a machine

questions.explanation: The transparency obligations require that people know they are talking to an AI system, and that AI-generated content such as deepfakes is identifiable. questions.prompt: Which practice is prohibited under the AI Act?

Spam filtering of incoming mail
Social scoring
Credit scoring with human oversight

questions.explanation: Social scoring is among the prohibited practices classed as unacceptable risk. questions.prompt: An employer at Rushmere Works wants AI that infers employees' emotions during meetings to rate their engagement. How does the AI Act treat emotion recognition in the workplace?

options.text: It is a high-risk use with safeguards
It needs a transparency notice alone
It is a prohibited practice
It is a minimal-risk use

Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Source: European Commission · AI Act regulatory framework.

questions.prompt: From which date do the AI Act's rules for stand-alone high-risk use cases apply, according to the Commission page checked on 14 Nov 2026?

2 December 2027
2 August 2026

2 August 2025
2 August 2026

questions.prompt: It is November 2026. Which AI Act obligations already apply to a company in the EU that deploys a public chatbot?

questions.prompt: Which of these is a duty of a provider of a high-risk AI system?

Publication of the model weights for inspection by the public
Human oversight, logging and detailed documentation
Free access for all users

questions.explanation: The Commission lists risk assessment and mitigation, high-quality datasets, activity logging, documentation, information for deployers, human oversight, and robustness and accuracy. questions.prompt: A governance lead says 'we follow the NIST framework, so we comply with the EU AI Act'. What is wrong with that?

The Act applies to model providers alone
Both are optional documents, so neither of them creates a duty to comply

questions.prompt: In a power-interest grid, how should a stakeholder with high power but low interest in an AI initiative be managed?

A team in another value stream that may reuse it later
An internal newsletter editor who reports on AI
A supplier whose tool is one option among several

questions.prompt: What separates a position from an interest in a stakeholder conflict?

A position can change, but an interest is fixed for good
A position is what someone demands; an interest is why
A position is formal, while an interest is personal and private

questions.prompt: Security wants every AI tool blocked until a full review, and a product team wants to start this week. Which approach resolves the conflict best?

options.text: Block the tool until the review has fully finished
Let the more senior of the two leaders decide the question alone
Agree a low-risk scope that can start now while the review runs
Start this week and inform security after launch

questions.explanation: A bounded, low-risk start meets the product team's need for speed and security's need for control, because the review continues before scope widens. questions.prompt: Which conflict-handling style seeks a solution that fully meets both parties' concerns?

options.text: Accommodating
Collaborating
Compromising
Avoiding

questions.explanation: Collaborating looks for an outcome that satisfies both sides, which takes more time but suits important issues with long-term relationships. questions.prompt: Two leaders each accept half of what they wanted on AI review rules to close a long dispute. Which style is this?

options.text: Collaborating
Compromising
Avoiding
Competing

Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When is a competing style appropriate in an AI conflict?

options.text: When more information is needed before anyone decides
When the issue matters little and harmony matters more
When both parties' concerns can be fully met together
When a firm decision is needed fast on safety

questions.explanation: Asserting one position firmly suits urgent issues where safety or compliance is at stake and there is no time for long negotiation. A list of every stakeholder's personal preferences

questions.prompt: Why should an AI initiative have one accountable owner rather than several?

Regulators forbid naming more than one owner for any AI system

Shared ownership blurs who decides and who answers

questions.prompt: Legal, risk and product keep reopening decisions already made about an AI tool. What would help most?

A decision log and a rule for revisiting them
Moving the decisions to a private email thread
More meetings so that each group can be heard again and again

questions.prompt: What does 'disagree and commit' mean in a stakeholder group?

Members commit just to the parts they agree with

questions.prompt: Frontline staff fear that an AI tool will cut their jobs, and they slow its rollout. What should the Value Architect do first?

Tell staff that the fear is groundless and move on
Hear the concern and give honest answers about the impact

questions.prompt: Why is AI hype a risk to stakeholder alignment?

Hype is only a problem for the marketing team
Hype makes AI tools illegal to buy in some markets

questions.prompt: Which step best aligns an AI initiative with the portfolio's strategy?

Choosing whichever AI model the central strategy team prefers most
Linking its outcome to a strategic theme and its key results
Asking each team to add AI to its iteration goals

questions.prompt: In a stakeholder workshop, two groups talk past each other about 'risk'. What should the facilitator do?

Ask each group to describe its risk with an example
Pick the definition used by the more senior of the two groups
Move on and return to the topic another day

questions.prompt: Why involve risk and compliance early in an AI initiative?

questions.prompt: What is a stakeholder map for?

Listing the AI tools that each department has bought this year so far

Showing the reporting lines of the AI programme team

questions.prompt: A Business Owner wants an AI feature in three months; the team estimates six. What is the best way to align?

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of airing conflicts in a shared forum rather than in private side conversations?

Everyone sees the trade-offs and shapes the decision

questions.prompt: Which behaviour damages trust between the Value Architect and stakeholders fastest?

Promising what the evidence does not support
Asking stakeholders to explain their concerns
Admitting uncertainty about a pilot's outcome

questions.prompt: An executive sponsor changes the AI initiative's goal every month. What should the Value Architect do?

Follow each change without comment so that the sponsor stays happy

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a decision log for an AI initiative?

Recording the AI model's decisions in production

questions.prompt: Why should a Value Architect separate the people from the problem in a heated AI debate?

questions.prompt: A data owner refuses to share data for an AI pilot. What should the Value Architect explore first?

questions.prompt: Which practice keeps stakeholders aligned during a long AI initiative?

questions.prompt: A conflict about an AI tool keeps returning after it seemed settled. What does this suggest?

The conflict is a normal part of AI work and can be ignored
