questions.prompt: A Value Architect runs an alignment workshop for an AI initiative. Which outcome should the workshop aim for?

options.text: A ranking of stakeholders by how supportive they are
Shared agreement on the problem, goals and limits
A detailed task plan for each team for the year
A final choice of AI vendor and contract terms

questions.explanation: Alignment means a common understanding of why the initiative exists, what success looks like and what limits apply. Vendor choice and detailed plans follow from that. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why can an avoiding style be harmful for an AI initiative?

options.text: It forces a vote on each disagreement in the group
Avoiding is not one of the recognised conflict-handling styles at all
Unresolved concerns resurface later as blockers or rework
Avoiding conflict makes the stakeholders angrier at once

questions.explanation: Avoiding postpones the issue, so it often returns at a worse time, such as just before launch. It is a recognised style, useful only for trivial issues or when time is needed to gather facts. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which stakeholders should confirm that an AI solution fits the way work is really done?

options.text: The vendor's solution architect for the product
The external auditors who review the controls
The people who will use it in their daily work
The chief financial officer who approves the budget

questions.explanation: Only the people doing the work know how it really happens, including the workarounds that documents miss. Their confirmation prevents solutions that look right but do not fit. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes alignment in SAFe terms?

options.text: Everyone agrees with every decision before it is made
Everyone follows the same detailed plan without change
Everyone reports to the same manager in the hierarchy
Everyone understands and works toward the same goals

questions.explanation: Alignment, one of SAFe's core values, means shared understanding of the mission and goals, so people can make consistent local decisions. It does not require one fixed plan or unanimous agreement. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A steering group has twelve members and rarely decides anything about the AI initiative. What would help?

options.text: Adding more members so that no view is left out
Letting the AI tool choose between the options
A few people with clear decision rights
Meeting less often to reduce the pressure on members

questions.explanation: Large groups without clear decision rights tend to discuss rather than decide. A small decision group that consults widely keeps both speed and inclusion. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a Value Architect understand each stakeholder's incentives?

options.text: Stakeholders must disclose their bonuses to the team
Incentives matter for HR, not for AI initiatives
People back changes that help them meet their goals
Incentives decide which AI tools are legal to use

questions.explanation: Knowing what each stakeholder is measured on shows how the initiative can help them, or why they might resist, which makes alignment practical. Their bonuses are their own business; their goals are not. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which opening line works best in a conversation with a sceptical stakeholder about an AI pilot?

options.text: Our competitors are already ahead of us on this.
What would you need to see to judge whether this works?
This pilot will change the way your team works forever.
The board has decided, so we need your support now.

questions.explanation: Inviting the sceptic to define the evidence they need turns them into a co-designer of the test. Pressure, fear and authority produce compliance at best. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Stakeholder alignment and conflict management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is rolling-wave planning?

options.text: Planning each phase once the last is finished
Planning near-term work in detail and later work roughly
Planning the whole initiative in full detail at the very start
Replanning from scratch at the end of each week

questions.explanation: Rolling-wave planning details what is close and certain and keeps the rest coarse, refining it as knowledge grows. It suits AI initiatives, where much is learned during the first increments. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI initiative is very uncertain about whether the data can support it. What should the first increment aim to do?

options.text: Sign a three-year contract with the chosen vendor
Answer the biggest unknown as cheaply as possible
Build the user interface so stakeholders see progress
Deliver the full solution to a small group of users

questions.explanation: Adaptive planning tackles the riskiest assumption first, here the data, because if it fails the rest of the work is wasted. A polished interface gives the illusion of progress. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do kill criteria help an AI initiative?

options.text: They are a legal requirement for all AI projects
They make stopping easier when evidence says it fails
They punish teams whose pilots do not succeed
They let the sponsor cancel the initiative for any reason

questions.explanation: Agreeing in advance what result would end the initiative removes the emotion and sunk-cost thinking from the decision later. Stopping early frees money and people for better ideas. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which four responses to a risk are commonly used in risk management?

options.text: Audit, activate, optimise and centralise
Avoid, reduce, transfer and accept
Plan, build, test and release
Ignore, hide, delay and deny

questions.explanation: Risks are avoided by not doing the risky thing, reduced by controls, transferred, for example by insurance or contract, or accepted when the cost of acting exceeds the benefit. Audit to centralise is the course's playbook, not a risk response. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company buys insurance against losses from an AI vendor outage. Which risk response is this?

options.text: Avoid
Transfer
Reduce
Accept

questions.explanation: Insurance and contractual indemnities move the financial impact of a risk to another party, which is transfer. The outage can still happen. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company decides against using AI for medical diagnoses at all, because the harm could be severe. Which risk response is this?

options.text: Reduce
Transfer
Accept
Avoid

questions.explanation: Choosing not to do the risky activity is avoidance. Reducing would mean using AI with controls, such as a clinician reviewing each output. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How should the level of human oversight for an AI use case be set?

options.text: By how much the AI tool costs per month
By the harm a wrong output could cause
By how senior the person who requested it is
By how new the AI model is on the market

questions.explanation: Oversight is proportionate to risk: outputs that could harm customers or breach rules need review, while harmless ones can run with monitoring. Cost and seniority do not change the harm. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is model drift?

options.text: A model's answers changing because of a prompt edit
A model moving from one cloud provider to another
Performance falling as real-world data changes
A model being replaced by a newer version each month

questions.explanation: Drift happens when the data a model sees in use moves away from the data it was built or tested on, so quality falls silently. It is why AI solutions need monitoring after launch. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice detects drift in a deployed AI solution?

options.text: Reviewing the vendor's release notes each quarter
Testing the model once before launch and never again
Asking users once a year whether they like the tool
Monitoring quality against a baseline over time

questions.explanation: Regular measurement against a baseline, for example on sampled outputs or a fixed evaluation set, shows when quality starts to slip. A single pre-launch test cannot. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant may be unavailable for hours if its vendor has an outage. What should the plan include?

options.text: A promise from the vendor that outages will not happen
A fallback way of working when the assistant is down
A rule that staff wait until the assistant returns
A second vendor running the same prompts at all times

questions.explanation: Business continuity for AI means knowing how work continues without the tool, at least for critical tasks. Promises cannot prevent outages, and full duplication is usually too costly. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should an AI risk register be revisited every PI rather than written once?

options.text: Each PI requires a new register by law in the EU
Registers expire under most audit rules after a PI
Rewriting it keeps the risk team busy and visible
Risks change as the solution, data and usage change

questions.explanation: New features, new data sources and wider use change both the likelihood and the impact of risks, so the register must evolve with the solution. A static register becomes a false comfort. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which of these risks is an adoption risk rather than a technical one?

options.text: The API rate limit is reached during peak hours
Staff keep using the old process instead
The model's accuracy falls on new types of input
The vector index grows too large for the database

questions.explanation: Adoption risks concern people and process: whether the solution is used and changes how work is done. Accuracy, rate limits and index size are technical risks. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does risk appetite describe?

options.text: How much the risk function costs each year
How many risks a team can list in its register
The risk accepted to reach a goal
How quickly the risk team responds to incidents

questions.explanation: Risk appetite sets how much risk the organisation is willing to take in pursuit of its objectives, which guides which AI use cases go first and how much control each needs. It is set by leadership, not by the risk register. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Two AI use cases offer similar value, but one carries far more regulatory risk. With a low risk appetite, which should go first?

options.text: The lower-risk one, while the other is de-risked
Neither, since any regulatory risk is unacceptable
Both at once, to save time on planning and setup
The higher-risk one, since it is more interesting

questions.explanation: With equal value, a low appetite points to starting with the safer option and using the time to reduce the other's risk. Refusing all regulatory risk would rule out most useful work. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a plan for an AI initiative include explicit decision points?

options.text: So that budgets can be spent in full before each point
So evidence leads to a choice to continue, change or stop
So that the sponsor can add scope at each decision point
So that teams can stop working between decision points

questions.explanation: Decision points turn learning into action: at each one, the evidence is reviewed and the initiative continues, pivots or stops. Without them, initiatives drift on by default. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A pilot meets its accuracy target, but users find it slow. What does adaptive planning suggest?

options.text: Address speed in the next increment, then reassess
Ignore speed, since it was not in the original plan
Declare success, since the agreed target was met
Stop the initiative, since users are unhappy

questions.explanation: Adaptive plans respond to what is learned, including needs nobody listed at the start. Meeting one target does not make a solution usable, and one problem does not justify stopping. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question is a feasibility filter likely to ask before any code is written?

options.text: Which team member will present the final demo?
How will the launch be announced to the press?
Is the data available, good and allowed to be used?
Which colour scheme will the user interface use?

questions.explanation: Data availability, quality and permission are among the most common reasons AI initiatives fail, so checking them first avoids building on sand. The course names its Feasibility Filters without public detail; this item follows their stated purpose, de-risking an initiative before code is written. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in an AI-specific risk register?

options.text: A change of logo on the internal portal
Wrong but confident outputs reaching customers
Holiday cover for the project manager in August
Late delivery of office furniture for the team

questions.explanation: Plausible but wrong output is a risk particular to AI and deserves explicit treatment, such as review, grounding and monitoring. The other items are ordinary project logistics. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team wants to skip evaluation to hit a demo date. What is the main risk?

options.text: Nobody knows if it is fit for real use
The vendor will refuse to support the solution
The demo will take longer to set up than planned
The team will be unable to write a press release

questions.explanation: Without evaluation, an impressive demo can hide poor quality on real cases, and decisions are made on false confidence. That is how pilots end up in the proof of concept graveyard. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice limits the damage if an AI feature misbehaves after release?

options.text: A longer release cycle with fewer, larger releases
A feature toggle that can switch it off quickly
A press statement prepared in advance for incidents
A rule that only senior staff may use the feature

questions.explanation: Being able to turn a feature off at once, and fall back to the previous behaviour, limits harm while the cause is found. Larger, rarer releases make each failure bigger. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is an evaluation set for an AI solution?

options.text: The group of stakeholders who approve each release
The list of vendors evaluated during procurement
The dashboard that shows how often users log in
Real cases with expected results, used to test

questions.explanation: An evaluation set is a stable collection of representative cases with known good answers, run before each change and regularly in use, so quality can be compared over time. Without one, changes are judged by impression. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI initiative depends on a vendor's model that may change without notice. Which mitigation fits?

options.text: Trust the vendor to keep the model's behaviour the same
Pin the version and re-run evaluations before upgrading
Avoid testing so that changes are not noticed
Switch vendors every month to spread the risk

questions.explanation: Pinning a version where possible, and testing any new version against the evaluation set before switching, reduces the risk of silent behaviour changes. Trusting the vendor is not a control. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to translate AI risks into business terms for leaders?

options.text: Business terms hide the technical details from the leaders
Translation removes the need to mitigate the risks
Leaders can then weigh risk against value and decide
Leaders are not allowed to see technical risk reports

questions.explanation: The course promises to help Value Architects translate risk into strategy: leaders decide better when risks are stated in terms of customers, money, reputation and compliance. Translation clarifies; it does not hide. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which plan best fits an AI initiative whose value is clear but whose feasibility is uncertain?

options.text: A short spike to test it, then a decision
A full-scale build, since the value has been proven
A vendor contract signed before testing the idea
A year-long research phase before any decision

questions.explanation: When value is known but feasibility is not, a short, focused test of feasibility is the cheapest way to learn whether to proceed. Committing to a full build or a contract first bets on the unknown. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During an AI pilot, users start pasting confidential data into prompts. Which risk response comes first?

options.text: Transfer it to the vendor through the contract
Accept it, since the pilot is small and short
Avoid it by cancelling the pilot without discussion
Reduce it with guidance and data controls

questions.explanation: Clear guidance, approved tools and technical controls such as redaction reduce the risk while the pilot continues. Accepting a data leak is rarely acceptable, and a contract does not undo exposure. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does adaptive planning differ from simply having no plan?

options.text: It plans in short cycles and adjusts to evidence
It leaves all decisions to the delivery teams
It uses the same plan whatever the evidence shows
It avoids commitments of any kind to stakeholders

questions.explanation: Adaptive planning still sets goals, decision points and near-term plans; it simply revises them as evidence arrives. Having no plan gives stakeholders nothing to rely on. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which signal should trigger a re-plan of an AI initiative?

options.text: A new AI model announced by a different vendor
A change in the colour of the user interface
A stakeholder who missed the last review meeting
Evidence that a key assumption was wrong

questions.explanation: Plans rest on assumptions, so when evidence breaks one, the plan should change. New announcements elsewhere are interesting but do not invalidate the plan by themselves. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a pre-mortem used for in AI planning?

options.text: Imagining failure in advance to find risks early
Testing the model's accuracy before launch
Estimating the cost of each AI experiment
Reviewing a failed AI project after it has closed

questions.explanation: A pre-mortem assumes the initiative has failed and asks why, which surfaces risks people might not otherwise voice. A review after closure is a post-mortem. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which way of presenting an AI risk helps leaders decide fastest?

options.text: Likelihood, impact, and options with costs
A long list of every possible failure in the system
A summary saying the risk is under control
A technical log of the model's errors last week

questions.explanation: Leaders need to know how likely and how bad a risk is, and what each response would cost, to make a decision. Exhaustive lists and reassurance do not support a choice. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should high-risk AI use cases start with a person in the loop even if automation is the goal?

options.text: It builds evidence of safe behaviour first
People in the loop make the AI model more accurate
Regulators ban automation for any use case at the start
Automation is never allowed for high-risk use cases

questions.explanation: Human review at first catches errors and produces data on how often the AI is right, which justifies, or rejects, more autonomy later. Autonomy should follow evidence. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Adaptive planning and risk management”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does total cost of ownership include for an AI solution?

options.text: The licence price paid in the first year alone
The vendor's quoted price minus any discounts
The cost of the pilot, which predicts all later costs
Build, run, monitor and support costs over its life

questions.explanation: AI solutions keep costing after launch: usage-based fees, monitoring, evaluation, retraining or re-prompting and support. Investment cases that count only the build or the first licence understate cost. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which funding approach suits an AI initiative with uncertain value?

options.text: Fund whichever team asks first and loudest
Fund small steps, releasing more as evidence grows
Fund nothing until the value is certain
Fund the full amount up front to show commitment

questions.explanation: Incremental funding, tied to evidence at each step, limits the money at risk while keeping the option to scale. It mirrors SAFe's approach of funding MVPs and deciding to pivot or persevere. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should an investment case for AI state its assumptions explicitly?

options.text: So the riskiest ones can be tested first
So auditors can approve the case without review
So that nobody can change the case later
So the case looks more thorough to the sponsor

questions.explanation: Named assumptions, such as data quality or adoption rates, become the hypotheses the first increments test. Hidden assumptions fail silently. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which benefit is strongest in an investment case for an AI support assistant?

options.text: The company appearing innovative in the press
Lower costs, assumed but not yet measured
Staff feeling more modern because they use AI tools
Shorter resolution times, measured against a baseline

questions.explanation: A benefit measured against a baseline can be checked and trusted. Feelings and reputation may matter, but they are weak grounds for investment. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is an AI inventory or register used for in governance?

options.text: Counting the number of prompts each employee writes
Tracking the training courses that each team has done
Listing the AI vendors that the company may want to buy from
Knowing which AI systems exist and who owns them

questions.explanation: Governance starts with visibility: a register of AI systems, their purpose, risk level and owner lets the organisation apply the right controls and answer regulators. Vendor lists and prompt counts are not governance. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which governance practice scales best as AI use grows across many teams?

options.text: Risk tiers, with light approval for low-risk uses
A ban on AI outside a single approved pilot team
No governance, so that teams can move as fast as possible
One central board that approves every AI use in person

questions.explanation: Tiering by risk focuses scarce review effort on high-risk uses and lets low-risk ones proceed quickly within guardrails. A single board becomes a bottleneck. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does good AI governance speed teams up rather than slow them down?

options.text: Governance lets teams ignore security reviews
Clear rules let teams act without asking each time
Governance removes the need for any testing of AI
Governance teams do the AI work on the teams' behalf

questions.explanation: When criteria are published and simple, teams can decide most cases themselves and know when to escalate. Unclear rules cause either delay or risky guesswork. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which standard specifies a management system for AI in an organisation?

options.text: ISO/IEC 42001
ISO 9001
ISO/IEC 27001

questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 42001 sets requirements for an AI management system. ISO 9001 covers quality management, ISO/IEC 27001 information security, and ISO 14001 environmental management. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Under the EU AI Act, a company uses an AI tool built by another firm in its own HR process. In which role is the company?

options.text: Distributor
Deployer
Provider
Importer

questions.explanation: The Act distinguishes providers, who develop AI systems and place them on the market, from deployers, who use them under their own authority. Deployers of high-risk systems have their own duties, such as human oversight. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Source: European Commission · AI Act regulatory framework.

questions.prompt: Which governance artefact records an AI system's intended use, limits and test results?

options.text: A RACI chart
A model card
A risk appetite statement
A vendor scorecard

questions.explanation: Model cards document what a model is for, how it was evaluated and where it performs poorly, which supports transparency and approval decisions. A RACI chart records roles. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An investment case shows high value but ignores the cost of keeping humans in the loop. What is the risk?

options.text: The value will rise further once humans are removed
The model will refuse to work with human reviewers
Humans in the loop are not allowed for high-value cases
Running costs are understated, flattering the return

questions.explanation: Human review is often a large part of an AI solution's running cost, especially at first. Leaving it out overstates the return and can kill the case later. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who should approve a high-risk AI use case in a well-governed organisation?

options.text: Anyone on the team, as long as they are trained
A named owner, with risk and legal involved by policy
The developer who built the first prototype of it
The vendor whose model the use case relies on

questions.explanation: High-risk uses need clear accountability and the right expertise, defined in policy. Builders and vendors have a stake in approval and cannot be the check. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows whether an AI investment is paying off?

options.text: The number of models the team has deployed
The number of employees who have logged in to the tool
The amount spent on licences this quarter
Change in the target outcome against the baseline

questions.explanation: Return is judged by the outcome the investment was meant to change, measured against where it started. Logins, spend and model counts are activity. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should governance for generative AI cover the prompts and data sent to external services?

options.text: Sensitive data can leave the organisation through prompts
External services do not accept prompts from companies
Prompts are protected by copyright and cannot be shared
Governance only needs to cover the model's final outputs

questions.explanation: Prompts often contain customer, employee or confidential business data, and sending them to external services is a data transfer that needs rules. Governing outputs alone misses that exposure. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team wants to switch to a cheaper model mid-project. What should governance require first?

options.text: Re-running evaluations to confirm quality holds
No check, since cost savings need no approval
Approval from each stakeholder on the project
A new business case written from the very beginning

questions.explanation: A model change can alter behaviour in ways that matter, so the evaluation set is run again before switching. A full new business case is out of proportion. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which governance step should come before an AI tool is connected to customer data?

options.text: A data protection impact check and an approval
An upgrade to the newest version of the model
A press release announcing the new connection
A team celebration of the successful integration

questions.explanation: Connecting AI to personal data changes the privacy risk, so an impact assessment and approval come first. Many regulators expect this for new uses of personal data. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An investment case compares an AI solution with doing nothing. Which other option should it also compare?

options.text: Buying both solutions and running them in parallel
A simpler non-AI improvement to the same process
A more expensive AI solution from a rival vendor
Delaying the decision for another full year

questions.explanation: Sometimes a process change or simple automation delivers most of the value at a fraction of the cost. A fair investment case shows why AI beats that option. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do sound AI investment cases include a measurement plan?

options.text: Without one, nobody can tell if value arrived
They let the sponsor claim success at any time
Measurement plans are required to buy AI licences
They replace the need for a baseline of any kind

questions.explanation: A measurement plan defines the baseline, the measures and when they will be reviewed, so the promised value can be confirmed or refuted. It depends on a baseline rather than replacing one. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which approach to AI governance fits SAFe's Lean-Agile principles best?

options.text: Guardrails and decentralised decisions within them
Central approval of each AI prompt before it is used
No rules, since teams know their work best
Annual audits as the single control on AI use

questions.explanation: SAFe favours guardrails with decentralised decision-making: central rules for what is infrequent and high-impact, and local decisions for the rest. Approving each prompt centralises the wrong decisions. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A governance board meets quarterly, and teams wait months for AI approvals. What should change?

options.text: Ask the board to meet once a year to reduce its workload
Let teams skip approval whenever the board is busy
Delegate low-risk decisions within clear criteria
Stop all AI work until the board can meet more often

questions.explanation: Delegating low-risk decisions with clear criteria removes the queue while the board focuses on high-risk cases. Skipping approval informally removes control altogether. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · The investment case and governance”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In which order does the course name the phases of the AI-Native solution lifecycle?

options.text: Discover, Sense, Deliver, Design
Design, Discover, Deliver, Sense
Sense, Discover, Design, Deliver
Sense, Design, Discover, Deliver

questions.explanation: The certification page names the phases as Sense, Discover, Design and Deliver. Source: Scaled Agile · AI-Native Value Architect certification page.

questions.prompt: What do the Sense, Discover, Design and Deliver phases turn a vague mandate into?

options.text: A signed contract with a model provider for the new solution
A production deployment in one step
A finalized, cross-functional AI-Native Value Blueprint
A portfolio epic with full funding

questions.explanation: The public description says the phases turn a vague mandate into a finalized, cross-functional AI-Native Value Blueprint. questions.prompt: An AI drafting tool at Tolworth Media is built in one large release after nine months, and users reject it. What would iterative delivery have changed?

Answers for one topic area, with sources, for a small group of users

questions.prompt: Before delivery starts at Upwell Health, the Value Architect checks whether records are complete, accessible and permitted for use. Which kind of readiness is this?

questions.prompt: Nobody at Varley Pay has decided who will monitor an AI solution's quality after launch or respond when it degrades. Which readiness gap is this?

questions.prompt: Enthusiasm for an AI programme at Wickham Rail fades three months after a good start. What sustains momentum best?

A stricter usage policy
A single annual showcase event held for the executive team
A new logo for the programme

questions.prompt: A team wants to automate a claims process end to end in its first release. What does iterative delivery suggest?

questions.prompt: What makes a good quick win for an AI initiative?

Large, ambitious and announced before it starts

questions.prompt: Which increment best follows a successful first release of an AI assistant for one policy area?

Rebuild the whole assistant on a larger model from scratch

Each one tests assumptions before more money is spent

Small increments need no testing or review

Release the next increment exactly as planned

questions.prompt: What does a minimum viable product test in AI delivery?

Whether the vendor's model is the best on the market

Measured results make it evidence that others will trust

questions.explanation: A measured win, with a baseline, convinces sceptics and sponsors in a way an announcement cannot, and it shows whether the win is worth scaling. questions.prompt: How does momentum relate to adoption of an AI solution?

A regular demo of progress to users

questions.prompt: Which practice keeps an AI solution ready as data and needs change?

questions.prompt: Which structure has the most impact with a senior audience?

options.text: The technology, the architecture, the roadmap, and then finally the benefit
The team members, the tools, and the timeline
A list of all metrics collected
The problem, what was done, the measured result, and the next decision

questions.explanation: A story that opens with the problem the audience recognises and ends with a decision they can make is the one that moves them. Leading with technology loses them before the benefit appears. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a results story include a specific person or team affected by the change?

options.text: Named individuals can then be held responsible for the outcome
Concrete examples make the numbers credible and memorable
It removes the need for data
It makes the presentation longer

questions.explanation: A single case that the audience can picture gives meaning to the aggregate figures. The example supports the data; it does not replace it. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: The same pilot result must be presented to engineers and to the finance director. What should change?

options.text: Nothing; one deck suits both
The figures, so that each audience hears what it prefers to hear
The emphasis and language, while the facts stay the same
The conclusion

questions.explanation: Each audience cares about different consequences of the same facts, so the framing adapts. Changing the figures by audience destroys trust the first time the two compare notes. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows the value of an AI assistant for support agents?

options.text: Change in resolution time and customer satisfaction against a baseline
Number of prompts sent to the assistant by the agents on each day of the week
Number of agents with a licence
Number of features in the assistant

questions.explanation: Value shows in the outcome the assistant was meant to improve, compared with what it was before. Prompt counts measure activity and can rise while outcomes stay flat. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Source: SAFe · AI Value Architect.

questions.prompt: What is a baseline when judging value?

options.text: The first version of the model
The target that the sponsor hopes to reach
The minimum budget for the pilot
The measured state before the change

questions.explanation: A baseline is the level of the measure before the change, against which improvement is judged. Without it, a result cannot be attributed to the initiative. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Aldgate Insurance reports faster claims handling, but no measurement was taken beforehand. What can be concluded?

options.text: The pilot failed
Little, since there is nothing to compare the result with
The pilot succeeded, because the handlers say it feels much faster
The model is accurate

questions.explanation: Without a baseline, the improvement is an impression. This is the value not measured cause that leaves pilots unable to justify scaling. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pair gives a balanced view of an AI solution's value?

options.text: Two satisfaction surveys of the project team
An early usage signal and a later business outcome
Two usage counts from the same dashboard
Two financial results taken a year apart

questions.explanation: A leading indicator shows early whether the change is taking hold, and a lagging outcome confirms the business effect. Two measures of the same kind leave half the picture missing. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Usage of an AI tool at Bramhall Bank is high, but the outcome it was meant to improve has not moved. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: The outcome measure should be dropped
The initiative has succeeded, since high usage was the agreed goal
The tool needs more users
Adoption is not the same as value; examine how the tool is used

questions.explanation: High usage with no outcome change suggests the tool is used for low-value tasks or its output is discarded downstream. Declaring success on usage alone confuses activity with benefit. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI feature raises output per developer, but defects in production rise too. How should the effect be reported?

options.text: Report the defects to the team alone
Report both, since value includes quality as well as speed
Report neither until both improve
Report the output gain and investigate the defects separately later

questions.explanation: A measure of speed without its quality counterpart overstates the benefit. Leaders making a funding decision need the whole effect. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Colby Retail missed its target. What is the right way to communicate that?

options.text: Attribute the result to the work of the data team
Present the secondary metrics that happened to improve
State the result, what was learned, and the recommended decision
Delay the report until a better result is available

questions.explanation: Honest reporting with a recommendation keeps trust and lets leaders redirect money promptly. Switching to whichever metric improved is a habit that makes later good news unbelievable. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is a negative pilot result still valuable to the organisation?

options.text: It stops further spending on an idea the evidence does not support
It proves AI does not work here
It reduces the need for governance
It shows which of the teams should be removed from the later pilots

questions.explanation: An early, cheap 'no' is one of the main returns on a small experiment. It says something about one hypothesis, not about AI in general or the people involved. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How often should results from an AI initiative be shared with stakeholders?

options.text: After each model upgrade
When a stakeholder asks
On a regular cadence, including when there is little to show
Once, when the final outcome has been confirmed by the finance team

questions.explanation: Regular updates keep stakeholders aligned and make surprises small. Waiting for a final outcome leaves a long silence in which support drifts. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Staff at Dunstan Health fear an AI scheduling tool will be used to cut jobs. What should the communication include?

options.text: What will change in their work, what will not, and how they can shape it
The productivity targets that the new tool is expected to help the hospital achieve
A reminder that use is mandatory
Technical details of the model

questions.explanation: People adopt a change when they understand its effect on them and have a say in it. Leading with productivity targets confirms the fear the message needed to address. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A tool is deployed and trained on, yet people return to the old way within a month. What does organisational change require beyond rollout?

options.text: Removal of the old tool's documentation
A second training session that repeats the first session's content in full
A stronger mandate
Reinforcement: updated processes, measures and leadership behaviour

questions.explanation: A change holds when the surrounding system supports it: the process expects the new way, measures reflect it and leaders model it. Repeating the training treats a system problem as a knowledge gap. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which sign shows that an AI practice has become part of how an organisation works?

options.text: The vendor contract was renewed
New work is designed with it by default, without a special programme
Every employee has completed the course
A dedicated programme office reports on its usage to leaders each month

questions.explanation: A change is embedded when it no longer needs separate attention to continue. A programme office reporting on usage shows the change is still being pushed from outside. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A person in this role is asked what she contributes if she does not build models or own the budget. Which answer fits?

options.text: She uses data to show whether AI work is producing the intended value
She approves which teams may use AI
She guarantees that each one of the AI initiatives will be successful
She replaces the product manager

questions.explanation: Using data to measure success is one of the five areas of the role, with coaching, connecting and facilitating. No role can guarantee outcomes; this one makes them visible and improvable. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Source: SAFe · AI Value Architect.

questions.prompt: Leaders ask for the return on an AI coding assistant after one month. What is the most honest reply?

options.text: Decline to report until the year ends
Give a precise annual return, extrapolated from the first month's usage data
Report the vendor's published figures
Share early indicators now and say when outcome data will be meaningful

questions.explanation: Early signals are useful if they are labelled as such, with a date for firmer evidence. A precise annual figure from one month looks rigorous and is a guess. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which topic does the exam list under Value Realization and Organizational Change?

options.text: Iterative delivery and quick wins
Investment case and the governance of AI initiatives
Diagnosing gaps and enabling collaboration
Storytelling for impact

questions.explanation: The exam details page lists storytelling for impact, measuring value and communicating results for this domain. The investment case belongs to the strategy domain. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Source: Scaled Agile · Exam details: AI-Native Value Architect.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its kind.

options.text: Lagging outcome
Input, not a result
Baseline
Leading indicator
Guardrail

slots.text: Share of agents using the assistant each week
Resolution time last quarter, before the change

questions.explanation: Weekly usage signals early adoption, satisfaction after six months is an outcome, last quarter's figure is the baseline and licences are an input. questions.prompt: Which story structure best fits a short update to executives on an AI pilot?

options.text: A full chronology of the project from its very first day onward
Model, data, prompts and infrastructure, in that order
A list of the team members and their individual tasks
Situation, what changed, the result, and what we ask next

questions.explanation: Executives need the context, the change, the measured result and the decision asked of them, in that order and briefly. Technical structure and chronology bury the point. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which detail makes an AI results story most credible?

options.text: A specific number tied to a named team or process
A quote from the vendor about the model's power
A claim that the result will transform the industry
A chart of the model's training loss over time

questions.explanation: Concrete, attributable numbers can be checked and remembered. Vendor quotes and grand claims invite scepticism. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a results story include what failed?

options.text: Regulators require every story to list three failures
Failures are more interesting than successes to read
It lowers expectations so later results look better
Honesty about limits makes the successes believable

questions.explanation: Audiences trust a story that admits problems, because it sounds like reality. Hiding failures makes every claim look like marketing. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which opening line best grabs a sponsor's attention in an AI results story?

options.text: This project began in March with a kickoff
We used a large language model with retrieval
AI is the most important technology of our time
Claims now close in four days instead of nine

questions.explanation: Opening with the outcome the sponsor cares about earns attention for the rest of the story. Technology, history and generalities can follow, if at all. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In a story for impact, what role does the audience's goal play?

options.text: It sets the length of the presentation slides
It decides which results to lead with
It decides which model the team should have used
It has no role, since results speak for themselves

questions.explanation: The same pilot has different headlines for a finance director, an operations lead and frontline staff. Leading with what each audience is trying to achieve makes the story land. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A story about an AI pilot is aimed at frontline staff. Which emphasis fits?

options.text: The vendor's roadmap for the next three years
The return on investment for the shareholders
What changes in their day, and how it helps
The technical architecture of the solution

questions.explanation: Frontline staff care about how their work will change and whether it gets easier. Financial returns and architecture matter to other audiences. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do before-and-after comparisons strengthen a story for impact?

options.text: They let the storyteller choose the most flattering dates
They show the change against a known start
They make a story longer and more detailed for readers
They remove the need to explain how the change happened

questions.explanation: A baseline and an after measure make the size of the change visible and credible. They still need an honest account of what caused the change. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which visual best supports a story about faster claims handling?

options.text: A table of every claim processed during the pilot
A simple chart of the time taken, before and after
A diagram of the model's neural network layers
A photo of the team celebrating the release

questions.explanation: One clear chart of the key measure before and after makes the result obvious at a glance. Architecture diagrams and raw tables distract from it. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Beyond understanding, what does storytelling for impact aim to secure?

options.text: A longer budget meeting with the sponsors
Approval of the slide template by marketing
Decisions and action, such as funding
Applause at the end of the presentation

questions.explanation: The course describes the story as a way to secure funding and adoption. A story for impact ends with what the audience should decide or do. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team has strong results but presents them as a list of twenty metrics. What would improve the impact?

options.text: Lead with the two or three that matter most to the audience
Add more metrics so that nothing important is missed
Remove all numbers and describe the results in words
Present the metrics in alphabetical order so they are easy to find

questions.explanation: Too many metrics hide the result; picking the few that matter to this audience, with the rest available on request, makes the point clear. Adding more makes it worse. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a Value Architect tailor the same story for different audiences?

options.text: Each audience acts on different parts of the evidence
Tailoring hides weak results from the senior audience
Each audience should receive different facts about it
Stories must be different lengths by company policy

questions.explanation: Tailoring changes emphasis and language, not the facts: each audience hears the part of the evidence it can act on. Changing facts by audience destroys trust. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which closing line best ends a story aimed at securing funding to scale up?

options.text: AI will change everything we do in the future
Questions are welcome at any time after today
Thank you all for listening to our presentation
This budget gets us five more sites by June

questions.explanation: A story for impact ends with a specific ask and what it will achieve, so the audience knows what decision is needed. Thanks and slogans give them nothing to decide. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a protagonist in an AI results story?

options.text: The AI model, presented as the hero of the story
The sponsor who approved the initial budget
The vendor whose product made the result possible
A real user or team whose work changed

questions.explanation: A real person or team whose work changed makes the numbers human and relatable. Casting the model or the vendor as the hero misses why the change matters. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A results story claims the AI 'saved 5,000 hours'. What should the storyteller be ready to show?

options.text: The vendor's estimate of hours saved elsewhere
How it was measured and what the time went to
A promise that the figure will double next year
A photo of the team that saved the hours

questions.explanation: Saved hours are credible only with a clear measurement method and a value only if the time was used for something useful. A good storyteller has both ready. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main danger of an AI story that exaggerates its results?

options.text: Lost credibility when the real numbers emerge
Regulators may fine the storyteller personally
The story will be too long for the audience
The team may be asked to repeat the success

questions.explanation: Exaggeration is found out when results are checked or the solution scales, and the loss of trust affects every later initiative. Honest numbers protect the storyteller. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Storytelling for impact”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a leading indicator for an AI solution?

options.text: A measure chosen by the vendor of the AI model
An early signal that predicts the later outcome
A measure that is reported to senior leaders first
The final business result, measured a year later

questions.explanation: Leading indicators, such as the share of suggestions accepted, move early and point toward the outcome, so they guide decisions before the lagging result arrives. Who sees a measure first does not make it leading. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which is a lagging indicator for an AI support assistant?

options.text: Customer satisfaction after three months
Share of suggestions accepted each day
Number of prompts sent in the first week
Number of agents who tried it in week one

questions.explanation: Customer satisfaction over months is an outcome that appears late and reflects the real effect. Trial counts and acceptance rates are early signals. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pair of measures guards against an AI tool speeding work up at the expense of quality?

options.text: Handling time together with number of logins
Handling time with error or rework rate
Prompt count together with model version
Licence cost together with number of users

questions.explanation: Pairing a speed measure with a quality measure shows whether faster work is also good work. Logins, licences and prompt counts say nothing about quality. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should value measures be agreed before an AI pilot starts?

options.text: So the vendor can tune the model to the chosen measures
So the pilot can skip the baseline measurement step
So stakeholders have nothing to discuss at the review
So results cannot be bent to fit hopes later

questions.explanation: Measures chosen after the fact tend to be the ones that look good. Agreeing them in advance, with a baseline, makes the result a fair test. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A pilot shows a 30% speed-up, but only for the most experienced staff. How should value be reported?

options.text: As a failure, since most staff saw no improvement
By group, showing who benefits and who does not yet
As a 30% speed-up for all staff, to keep it simple
As a success for the vendor's model in general

questions.explanation: Reporting by group shows where the value is and where training or design changes are needed. A single average or a blanket verdict hides that. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When measuring an AI solution's value, what does the counterfactual mean?

options.text: What would have happened without the solution
What the vendor says the solution will achieve
What the solution did on the vendor's test data
What the users would like the solution to do

questions.explanation: Value is the difference between what happened and what would have happened anyway, for example through seasonal change. Comparison groups and baselines estimate the counterfactual. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which method gives the most trustworthy evidence of an AI tool's effect?

options.text: Counting how often the tool is opened each day
Asking the tool's sponsor how well it worked
Reading positive comments posted by early users
Comparing similar groups with and without it

questions.explanation: A comparison between similar groups separates the tool's effect from other changes happening at the same time. Opinions and usage counts cannot. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why can usage alone mislead about an AI solution's value?

options.text: Usage figures are inflated by the vendor's software
Usage cannot be measured for AI tools at all
People can use a tool a lot without better results
Usage matters to the finance department alone

questions.explanation: High usage shows adoption, not value: a tool can be used heavily and still not improve outcomes, or even make them worse. Outcome measures are needed alongside. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure best captures the value of an AI coding assistant?

options.text: Lines of code generated by the assistant each week
Percentage of suggestions shown to developers
Lead time for changes, with defect rates alongside
Number of developers with an active licence

questions.explanation: Faster delivery of working changes is the value, and defect rates check that quality held. Lines of code and licences measure activity. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a value hypothesis for an AI initiative?

options.text: A guess about which vendor will win the contract
A promise of value that does not need to be tested
A testable statement of the expected outcome
A forecast of the AI market's growth next year

questions.explanation: A value hypothesis states the expected outcome in measurable terms, so the initiative can be tested against it and stopped or scaled on evidence. A promise that needs no test is not a hypothesis. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI tool's benefit appears in another department's budget rather than the sponsor's. How should value be measured?

options.text: Across the whole flow, wherever it lands
In the vendor's case study, as an independent view
In the sponsor's budget only, since they paid for it
Not at all, since the benefit is hard to attribute

questions.explanation: Systems thinking measures value end to end: if the benefit lands elsewhere in the value stream, it is still value. Measuring only the sponsor's budget would undercount it. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why measure both early indicators and final outcomes for an AI initiative?

options.text: Early ones satisfy auditors; outcomes satisfy the vendor
Early ones guide decisions; outcomes confirm the value
Both are required by the EU AI Act for all systems
Final outcomes arrive first, so early ones confirm them

questions.explanation: Leading indicators give timely signals for pivot-or-persevere decisions, and lagging outcomes confirm whether the promised value arrived. Each alone is incomplete. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which baseline is needed to measure an AI tool that drafts customer replies?

options.text: The industry average handling time from a survey
Current handling time and quality, before launch
The handling time the sponsor expects after launch
The vendor's benchmark scores for its latest model

questions.explanation: A baseline is the organisation's own measured state before the change, covering the outcomes that matter, here time and quality. Benchmarks and expectations are not baselines. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Measuring value”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What should an AI results update include when results are mixed?

options.text: The negative results alone, to look objective
A note that results will be shared at the end
The positive results alone, to protect the funding
What worked, what did not, and what happens next

questions.explanation: A balanced update shows the full picture and the decision that follows from it. Selective reporting either way misleads the people who must decide. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which channel best communicates AI results to frontline staff?

options.text: A slide in the annual shareholder presentation
An email from the vendor's marketing department
A long written report posted on the intranet without any notice
A short demo in their team meeting, with time for questions

questions.explanation: Frontline staff engage best with a short, concrete demo in their own setting where they can ask questions. Unannounced reports and vendor emails rarely reach them. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why share results with the teams who use an AI solution as well as with sponsors?

options.text: It shows their effort matters and invites their ideas
Sponsors are not interested in AI results at all
It is required before the next licence renewal
Teams must approve results before sponsors can see them

questions.explanation: Users who see the results of their effort stay engaged and often suggest the next improvement. Keeping results at the top breaks that loop. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A sponsor asks for 'just the good news' in an AI update. How should the Value Architect respond?

options.text: Agree, since the sponsor decides what is reported
Explain why a balanced update protects the sponsor too
Refuse to send any update until the sponsor relents
Send the good news first and hide the rest in a long appendix

questions.explanation: Bad news hidden today surfaces later, often at a worse moment for the sponsor. Explaining that keeps the update honest while respecting the sponsor's concern. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a results dashboard for an AI initiative?

options.text: Reporting each team member's daily activity
Showing the model's internal workings in detail
Showing progress on agreed measures at any time
Replacing all conversations with stakeholders

questions.explanation: A dashboard makes progress against the agreed measures transparent and self-service. It complements, rather than replaces, conversations about what the results mean. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Results show that an AI tool helps one team a lot and another not at all. What should the update say?

options.text: No result until the second team's figures improve
Both results, with the reasons as far as they are known
The successful team's result alone, as the headline
The average across both teams, as a single overall figure

questions.explanation: Reporting both, with what is known about why, gives decision makers the real picture and points to what to fix. An average hides the difference. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should communication about AI results be regular rather than only at milestones?

options.text: Stakeholders forget about AI if they are not reminded
Milestones are not used in AI initiatives at all
Regular updates keep trust and catch problems early
Regular updates let the team avoid formal reviews

questions.explanation: Frequent, short updates mean nobody is surprised, and problems are raised while they are still small. Long gaps breed rumours and late shocks. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which message best communicates an AI result to the finance director?

options.text: The pilot used three times fewer tokens than planned
Cost per claim fell 12%, net of running costs
Staff said they enjoyed using the new AI tool
The model reached 94% accuracy on the test set

questions.explanation: Finance cares about net financial effect, including the AI's own running costs. Accuracy and satisfaction matter, but not as the headline for this audience. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What should each AI results update link the results to?

options.text: The outcomes and measures agreed at the start
The vendor's latest product announcement
The number of hours the team worked
The AI strategy of a competitor

questions.explanation: Linking results to the agreed outcomes shows progress against what was promised and keeps the story consistent over time. Vendor news and hours worked are not results. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Staff hear rumours that an AI pilot failed when in fact it met its goals. What should happen?

options.text: Share the actual results openly and promptly
Ask managers to stop staff discussing the pilot
Wait for the end-of-year review to correct the record
Ignore the rumours, since the results speak for themselves

questions.explanation: Rumours fill gaps in communication, so the fix is prompt, open sharing of the real results. Suppressing discussion makes people trust the rumour more. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a Value Architect communicate the next decision along with the result?

options.text: Decisions are more interesting to read than results
Results matter for what the business does next
The next decision must be approved by all readers
Results without decisions are not allowed in SAFe

questions.explanation: A result is useful when it informs a choice, such as scaling, adjusting or stopping. Saying what happens next turns information into action. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps results reach people across a large organisation?

options.text: Local champions who retell the story
A results page that nobody is told about
A single company-wide email from the AI team
A presentation to the executive team only

questions.explanation: Local champions translate results into their colleagues' context and answer questions in person, which spreads the message far better than one central broadcast. Unannounced pages reach almost nobody. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the 'so what' when communicating AI results?

options.text: The list of next steps for the delivery team
What a finding means for the listener's goals
A technical appendix explaining the metrics
A question the audience is not allowed to ask

questions.explanation: The 'so what' connects a number to what the listener cares about, which is what turns a fact into a reason to act. Without it, numbers are just numbers. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI initiative is stopped after its pilot. How should this be communicated?

options.text: As little as possible, to avoid embarrassment
As a success, by focusing on the positive parts
As the vendor's failure, to protect the team
As an evidence-based decision, with lessons

questions.explanation: Stopping on evidence is good governance and saves money; communicating it openly, with lessons, helps others and keeps trust. Spin or silence teaches people to hide failures. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Communicating results and making change last”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do communicated results matter for organisational change?
